summary: An informational memo describing the purpose, usage scenarios and requirements for the Transaction Internet Protocol.

eli5.summary: The list of reasons why a team-agreement tool is needed, and what it must be able to do.

questions: why do distributed applications need two-phase commit
subtitle: Why the Internet needed a two-phase commit protocol and what it must do.

tldr.problem: Distributed applications that need transactions were forced to use complex, specialized protocols tied to specific communication methods. This made it hard to use transactions with modern internet protocols like HTTP.
tldr.mechanism: TIP defines a simple two-phase commit protocol that runs independently from application communications. It can work with any protocol (HTTP, TCP/IP, ODBC) and supports a "two-pipe" model: one pipe for application data, another for transaction coordination.
tldr.outcome: Developers can now build transactional applications on the internet using standard web protocols, with transactions providing the guarantee that either all participants succeed or all roll back. This unlocked distributed transactions for web applications.

today: RFC 2372 is informational and describes requirements for the Transaction Internet Protocol (RFC 2371). While TIP itself saw limited adoption, the two-pipe model and protocol independence principles it advocates remain relevant for modern distributed transaction systems.

sections.title: The Problem with Current Transactions
sections.content:
Transactions are a powerful programming tool: they guarantee atomicity, meaning either all parts of a distributed unit of work succeed or all roll back, leaving no partial results. This property makes distributed applications much simpler to write.

However, existing two-phase commit (2-pc) protocols used by transaction monitors and databases are tightly bound to a single communication mechanism. The standard protocols (OSI TP, LU6.2) are complex with large footprints and extensive configuration requirements. More importantly, they prevent applications from using modern internet protocols like HTTP. An application that wants transactions is forced into a special environment with a particular protocol stack, limiting flexibility and interoperability.

This memo describes TIP, which solves this by separating transaction coordination from application communication. Unlike traditional protocols that bind transaction messages and application messages into a single "pipe", TIP uses a "two-pipe" model: one pipe carries the application messages (over HTTP, ODBC, or any other protocol), while a separate pipe carries transaction coordination messages.
sections.eli5: Old transaction protocols were like a locked container that only worked with one type of communication. TIP is more like a separate agreement system that works on top of any kind of communication.

sections.title: The Two-Pipe Model and TIP Components
sections.content:
The two-pipe model is TIP's core innovation. Pipe 1 carries application communication (the actual work being done), while Pipe 2 carries TIP two-phase commit messages (the agreement about whether to commit or roll back). This separation allows any application protocol to be used with TIP transactions.

TIP defines two classes of compliant transaction managers. Client-only systems provide an application interface to begin and end transactions but do not manage local resources. These lightweight implementations delegate transaction coordination to a full server system, which manages recoverable resources, coordinates the two-phase commit, and maintains a transaction log for recovery.

The protocol operates in phases. In the commit phase, the coordinator sends PREPARE commands to all participants. Participants prepare their local resources and respond PREPARED if successful. Once all participants are prepared, the coordinator sends COMMIT commands. If any participant fails during preparation, the coordinator aborts the entire transaction.
sections.eli5: The two pipes are like having two phone lines: one for talking about what to do, one for making the actual deal official. The transaction manager is like an auctioneer that asks everyone if they can deliver, then either says 'go ahead' or 'cancel it'.

sections.title: Nine Key Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 2372 identifies nine requirements that TIP must satisfy. First, protocol independence: TIP must work with any application communication protocol, enabling transactions for HTTP, ODBC, plain TCP/UDP, or any future protocol. Second, transaction semantics: TIP must provide the presumed-abort two-phase commit protocol, guaranteeing atomicity even when failures occur, and support construction of the transaction tree.

Third, propagation and interoperability: TIP transactions must be propagatable via URLs that contain the transaction coordinator's address and transaction identifier, allowing applications to join an existing transaction. Fourth, simplicity: the protocol should include only necessary features, not extraneous optimizations.

Fifth, suitability for all applications: TIP must work for both ultra-lightweight clients and high-throughput enterprise systems, support client-only participants, allow transaction coordination delegation, scale to multiple concurrent transactions per connection, and support command pipelining.

Sixth, security: TIP must be compatible with encryption (TLS), authentication, and firewall mechanisms. Seventh, transport independence: TIP should not preclude use with transport protocols other than TCP. Eighth, recovery: recovery semantics must be defined to avoid ambiguous results after failures. Ninth, extensibility: TIP must be extendable while maintaining backward compatibility.
sections.eli5: TIP needs to work with any phone system, be simple, work for tiny and huge systems, be secure, survive problems, and be upgradeable.

sections.title: An Example: The Travel Agency Scenario
sections.content:
RFC 2372 uses a travel agency example to illustrate TIP. A client visits a travel agency web page and selects flights and hotels. When the client clicks 'book', the following happens:

The travel agency begins a transaction and obtains a TIP URL containing the transaction coordinator's address and a transaction identifier. The agency sends this URL to the airline server along with a booking request. The airline uses the TIP URL to join the transaction with a tip_pull() call, creating a local subordinate transaction and connecting to the agency's transaction manager. Work proceeds (the airline checks availability and reserves a seat), and the airline returns success. Steps are repeated with the hotel server.

Once all work is complete, the travel agency calls commit(). The coordinator sends PREPARE commands to both the airline and hotel. Each subordinate coordinator prepares its local resources (locks data, creates recovery logs) and responds PREPARED. The superior coordinator logs the decision to commit, sends COMMIT commands, and both subordinates commit their resources and respond COMMITTED. The transaction is now resolved: either all participants committed or (if any failed during prepare) all rolled back.
sections.eli5: The travel agent is the coordinator. It asks the airline 'Can you book a flight?' and the hotel 'Can you book a room?' When both say yes, the agent says 'Okay, go ahead!' and the deal is done.

sections.title: Recovery and Durability
sections.content:
Until a transaction reaches the Prepared state, any failure causes the transaction to abort. Once prepared, recovery must be performed. For the coordinator: before sending COMMIT, it must create a commit-recovery-record in its log. It must not forget the transaction until it has received COMMITTED responses from all subordinates. For subordinates: before responding PREPARED, they must create a prepared-recovery-record in their log. They must not forget the transaction until they receive a COMMIT or ABORT command.

If a connection fails after a subordinate has responded PREPARED but before receiving COMMIT, the superior can later send a RECONNECT command. The subordinate responds RECONNECTED if it still has the transaction in Prepared state, and the superior then sends COMMIT. If the subordinate has forgotten the transaction, it responds NOTRECONNECTED. Alternatively, if the subordinate's connection restores first, it can send a QUERY command, and the superior responds QUERIEDEXISTS or QUERIEDNOTFOUND.

The memo also notes that if a failure prevents the client from receiving a response to its commit request, even though the transaction succeeded, the client must use an implementation-specific mechanism (such as a user-visible log) to determine the outcome.
sections.eli5: Everyone writes down what happened so that if the phone call breaks, they can pick up where they left off. Either they remember and continue, or they forgot and say 'I do not know about that'.
